### The Department of Lost Minutes

At 8:03 every morning, Mara unlocked the Department of Lost Minutes.

The department occupied a narrow office between a bakery and a shop that sold only blue shoes. Its brass sign was easy to miss. Most people did miss it, which was perhaps why so many minutes remained lost.

Inside stood thousands of small drawers. Each was labeled in careful black ink:

**MISSED TRAINS**  
**UNSENT MESSAGES**  
**WAITING FOR KETTLES**  
**FORGOTTEN NAMES**  
**LOOKING OUT OF WINDOWS**  
**THINGS ALMOST SAID**

Mara’s job was to receive lost time, classify it, and—when possible—return it to its owner.

People lost minutes in all sorts of ways. Some dropped them while hurrying. Others abandoned them deliberately, usually in hospitals, airports, and uncomfortable conversations. Children rarely lost time. They stretched it too well.

At 8:17, the first customer entered.

He was an old man wearing a yellow scarf.

“I’ve misplaced an afternoon,” he said.

“An entire afternoon?”

“Yes. In June of 1974.”

Mara took out the necessary form.

“Do you remember where you last had it?”

“In a field, I think. There was a bicycle. And someone named Elise.”

“Weather?”

“Sunny. No—cloudy. It had just rained.”

“Emotional significance?”

The old man looked toward the drawers.

“Considerable.”

Mara led him into the archive. They searched under **SUMMERS**, then **FIRST LOVES**, then **DECISIONS POSTPONED UNTIL TOO LATE**. At last, behind a box of unasked questions, Mara found a pale green envelope.

The old man opened it.

The department filled with the smell of wet grass.

For a moment, Mara heard bicycle wheels turning on a dirt road. A young woman laughed somewhere beyond the walls.

The old man closed the envelope quickly.

“That’s it,” he whispered.

“Would you like to take it with you?”

He considered this. Then he shook his head.

“No. I only wanted to know it was real.”

After he left, Mara returned the envelope to its drawer.

At 10:42, a woman came in carrying a sleeping baby. She had lost seven hours.

“Last night?” Mara asked.

“Every night,” the woman replied.

Sleep was outside the department’s jurisdiction, but Mara gave her twenty quiet minutes from the emergency reserve. The woman sat in the back room while Mara held the baby. Neither spoke.

At noon, the bells above the door rang, though no one entered.

On the floor lay a single second.

It shone like a coin.

Mara picked it up with tweezers and examined it beneath the desk lamp. It was fresh, warm, and unusually heavy. A final second, perhaps. Or the second before a kiss. Those were nearly identical under ordinary light.

She placed it in an evidence jar.

By afternoon, the city had begun to rain. Water scribbled down the windows. Customers came and went.

A boy searched for the five minutes before he broke his mother’s vase.

A violinist asked whether twelve years spent practicing counted as lost.

A politician attempted to donate several decades that did not belong to him.

At 5:55, just before closing, a young woman entered. She wore a red coat darkened by rain.

“I’m looking for a minute,” she said.

“Which one?”

“The minute I decided not to come here.”

Mara set down her pen.

“If you decided not to come, how are you here?”

“I changed my mind.”

“That creates a separate minute.”

“I know. I lost that one too.”

Cases involving contradictory time required a supervisor, but Mara’s supervisor had departed nine years earlier for lunch and had not yet returned.

“Let’s begin with your name,” Mara said.

The woman hesitated.

“Mara.”

Outside, a bus passed through a puddle. The sound seemed very far away.

“That’s my name,” said Mara.

“I know.”

The woman took off her coat. She was older than she had first appeared. There were silver threads in her hair and a scar across her left palm—the same scar Mara had gotten at twelve while climbing a fence.

“You’re me,” Mara said.

“Eventually.”

“You look tired.”

“So do you.”

Mara glanced at the clock. The second hand trembled but did not advance.

“What minute did you lose?”

The older Mara looked around the office: the endless drawers, the careful labels, the jars filled with gleaming seconds.

“All of them,” she said. “One at a time.”

She explained that the department never closed, not really. There was always another customer, another vanished summer, another hour spent beside a bed. Mara would continue sorting everyone else’s time until she discovered that her own had quietly gone missing.

“Why didn’t anyone warn me?” Mara asked.

“I just did.”

The clock resumed.

5:56.

Rain tapped the glass.

Mara thought of the old man’s field, the sleeping woman, the violinist’s twelve years. She thought of all the time people called wasted simply because it had not become what they expected.

“What happens if I leave?” she asked.

“I don’t know,” said her older self. “I didn’t.”

Mara reached beneath the counter and found her coat.

Together, they stepped outside.

The bakery was closing. The blue-shoe shop had turned off its lights. Above the roofs, the clouds were breaking apart, revealing a narrow strip of gold.

Mara locked the department door.

At once, every clock in the city lost a minute.

No one complained.

The bakers stood in the warm doorway. Drivers lifted their feet from the pedals. In apartments and stations, in kitchens and corridors, people paused without knowing why.

For one unrecorded minute, nobody was late.

Mara breathed the rain-cooled air.

When she turned, her older self was gone.

In her place stood a girl with a bicycle, waiting at the corner.

“Are you coming?” the girl called.

Mara did not know where they were going.

That, she decided, was not the same as being lost.
